anchor: Much have I travell’d in the realms of gold
note: George Chapman’s English Homer (1616) was a famous translation of the Iliad and Odyssey. Keats read it with wonder and wrote this sonnet.

anchor: Which bards in fealty to Apollo hold
note: Fealty: loyalty owed to a lord. Bards hold the western islands as loyal servants of Apollo, god of poetry.

anchor: That deep-brow’d Homer ruled as his demesne
note: Demesne: land a lord keeps for himself, his own territory.

anchor: Yet did I never breathe its pure serene
note: Serene: here, a clear, calm sky or atmosphere.

anchor: When a new planet swims into his ken
note: Ken: range of sight or knowledge.

anchor: Or like stout Cortez
note: Keats names Cortez, but Palgrave notes that history requires Balboa, the Spaniard who first saw the Pacific from a mountain in 1513.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 166, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Balboa, Vasco Nuñez de”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Balboa%2C_Vasco_Nu%C3%B1ez_de

anchor: Look’d at each other with a wild surmise
note: Surmise: a guess, a half-formed idea about something unknown.

anchor: Silent, upon a peak in Darien
note: Darien is the eastern part of the isthmus joining Central and South America, now mostly in Panama. Balboa explored it in the 1510s.

anchor: Seated on Elysian lawns
note: Elysium was the Greek paradise of the blessed after death. Elysian therefore means heavenly and blissful, and here describes the lawns of the poets’ afterlife.

anchor: Browsed by none but Dian’s fawns
note: Dian is Diana, the Roman goddess of the moon and the hunt, whose companions were wild creatures.

anchor: Never slumber’d, never cloying
note: Cloying: so sweet or rich that one is sickened.

anchor: Their green felicity
note: Felicity: happiness, great joy. The trees’ green felicity is their happy, leafy state.

anchor: With a sleety whistle through them
note: Sleety: with rain frozen into small icy pellets.

anchor: Writhed not at passed joy?
note: Writhed: twisted in pain or distress, as a body does in agony or sorrow.

anchor: The sedge has wither’d from the lake
note: Sedge: a grasslike plant that grows by water.

anchor: So haggard and so woe-begone
note: Haggard: looking worn and gaunt. Woe-begone: overcome by sorrow.

anchor: The squirrel’s granary is full
note: Granary: a storehouse for grain, here the squirrel’s store of nuts.

anchor: And honey wild and manna-dew
note: Manna was the food that appeared miraculously on the ground for the Israelites in the desert.
source: Merriam-Webster, “manna”, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/manna; The Bible (King James Version), Exodus 16, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: She took me to her elfin grot
note: Grot: a grotto, a small cave.

anchor: Hath thee in thrall!
note: In thrall: in bondage, held as a slave.

anchor: I saw their starved lips in the gloam
note: Gloam: twilight, the evening dusk.

anchor: And this is why I sojourn here
note: Sojourn: to stay for a time.

anchor: Like Nature’s patient sleepless Eremite
note: Eremite: a hermit. Palgrave links the word to the fable of the Wandering Jew, who is doomed never to rest.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 198, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Of pure ablution round earth’s human shores
note: Ablution: a ritual washing, here the sea washing the shores.

anchor: Before my pen has glean’d my teeming brain
note: Glean’d: gathered bit by bit. Teeming: overflowing with ideas.

anchor: Hold like rich garners the full-ripen’d grain
note: Garners: storehouses for grain, so the books are like rich granaries.

anchor: Choicer than the Mermaid Tavern? Have ye tippled drink more fine
note: The Mermaid Tavern was a London inn where Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, and other writers of that age are said to have met.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 229, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Than mine host’s Canary wine
note: Canary wine: a sweet wine from the Canary Islands, popular in Shakespeare’s England.

anchor: Drest as though bold Robin Hood
note: Robin Hood is the outlaw hero of old English ballads who lived in the greenwood with his band and with Maid Marian.

anchor: The Mermaid in the Zodiac!
note: Zodiac: the band of twelve star-groups the sun passes through each year, each with a sign.

anchor: Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind
note: Winnowing: separating grain from chaff by blowing air through it. Autumn rests on the threshing floor, hair stirred by it.

anchor: Spares the next swath
note: Swath: the strip of grass or grain cut by one sweep of the scythe or hook.

anchor: like a gleaner thou dost keep
note: Gleaner: one who gathers leftover grain after the main harvest.

anchor: Among the river sallows
note: Sallows: willow trees, especially low shrubby ones.

anchor: from hilly bourn
note: Bourn: a stream, or a small brook, in southern English dialect.

anchor: The redbreast whistles from a garden croft
note: Croft: a small enclosed field or small farm next to a house.

anchor: Sit thee by the ingle
note: Ingle: a fire burning on a hearth, or the fireplace itself.

anchor: The sear faggot blazes bright
note: Sear: dry and withered. Faggot: a bundle of sticks bound for fuel.

anchor: From the ploughboy’s heavy shoon
note: Shoon: an old plural of shoe, here the farm boy’s heavy shoes.

anchor: She has vassals to attend her
note: Vassals: servants or subjects who owe loyalty to a lord. Fancy is pictured as a queen with a court.

anchor: Sweet birds antheming the morn
note: Antheming: singing like an anthem, a song of praise.

anchor: Dulcet-eyed as Ceres’ daughter
note: Dulcet: sweet to the ear or the senses, pleasant and soothing.
